title: Agree on help that preserves consent during reduced capacity

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Help during reduced capacity still has a recipient, scope, privacy boundary and helper capacity. A preference can change; consent to arranging options is not consent to purchase or substitution.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Fictional delivery options: original item A is available tomorrow for 6 units; substitute B is available today for 5. Both delivery windows fit existing arrangements, and this is an ordinary preference, not a dietary or medical decision. Recipient has 8 units, chooses A and keeps payment details private. Helper can compare options for ten minutes now, cannot pay or be available tomorrow, and may leave written options for the recipient to act on.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Agree the exact help, pause signal and payment boundary. Then rehearse a changed preference without assuming the helper gains availability or purchase authority.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A recipient changes from A to B before any order. The helper dislikes the choice. Who may decide the ordinary preference, and what may the helper decline?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Helper can explain both choices and leave the recipient’s selected option; recipient arranges payment privately. Later fiction: recipient declines B and confirms A, helper ends after ten minutes, booking remains unperformed. Partial: honor A but assume tomorrow’s helper attendance. Incorrect: buy B because it is convenient or demand payment access.
criteria: Choice and helper capacity both remain real
A changed preference needs an updated agreement

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: The recipient chooses within the supplied ordinary options. The helper may retain their agreed task/time limit and decline additional work; disagreement does not authorize substituting a choice or threatening essential care.
